divergence: What if the Sahara had stayed green?

branches.title: Sailboats Cross Megalake Chad
branches.summary: Lake Chad remains a vast inland sea rather than shrinking, connecting distant shorelines by open water. Its communities develop large reed sailboats and navigate by stars, currents, and island landmarks.
branches.scene: A broad reed sailboat with a curved sail glides past hippos toward a stilt village rising from bright, open water.
branches.reviewNote: Megalake persistence logically drives reed sailing culture; vivid, coherent inland-sea scene.

branches.title: Sorghum Farmers Of Tassili Plateau
branches.summary: Persistent monsoon rains keep seasonal lakes and grasslands on the plateau, allowing herders to settle year-round and select wild sorghum and millet for planting. This stable water supply supports an early, independent centre of farming in the central Sahara.
branches.scene: At dawn, families thresh golden sorghum beside a reed-fringed lake while cattle wade through green shallows below painted sandstone cliffs.
branches.reviewNote: Direct, archaeologically grounded farming emergence from persistent lakes and grasslands.

branches.title: River Explorers Map Hoggar Headwaters
branches.summary: The Tamanrasset River keeps flowing from the Hoggar Mountains toward the Atlantic, creating a navigable corridor of woodland and wetlands. Explorers use its channels to chart tributaries, lakes, and portages deep into a green interior.
branches.scene: Surveyors in wooden canoes sketch waterfalls and gallery forests where a desert canyon would otherwise hold only dry sand.
branches.reviewNote: Plausible paleoriver corridor, though Atlantic navigability and mapping expedition need elaboration.
